passage: I am Rekha, and I still remember the corridor of the junior hostel in my first month. Imran, a final-year senior, lined up the four of us and told us to make a shy new junior, Dev, stand on a chair and sing until told to stop. He called it tradition. I laughed louder than anyone so that nobody would pick me next. Dev's hands shook. Nisha looked at the floor. Aakash shook his head very slightly but said nothing. I told myself it was Imran's order, so it was Imran's doing, not mine. I felt lighter for about an hour. Later I could not remember Dev's song, only Dev's face.

qa.q: What did Imran tell the four juniors to make Dev do?
qa.a: Imran told them to make Dev stand on a chair and sing until told to stop.

qa.q: Why did Rekha laugh louder than anyone in the corridor?
qa.a: Rekha was afraid of being picked next, and comforted by the thought that it was Imran's order, not Rekha's doing; the lighter feeling lasted only about an hour before guilt came.

qa.q: What choice in the corridor could have protected Dev?
qa.a: Rekha could have refused to laugh, stepped away, or told the warden or a trusted teacher afterwards; one person disagreeing shows the others they do not have to join in.

qa.q: How might Dev have experienced that evening?
qa.a: Dev's shaking hands suggest fear and humiliation, with no sign that anyone would stand up for Dev.

grounding: A new junior does what a senior demands to avoid punishment, treating the senior as responsible, which is how harm gets done.

passage: Supervisor's note, intern week three. Deepak was told by Payal, a senior analyst, to enter the client figures again using her login because the deadline was close. He did, and when I asked, he said, "Payal said it was fine." Two other interns watched and said nothing. I spoke with Deepak privately that afternoon: nobody had threatened him, but he feared a bad reference. I told him it is fine to ask "is this okay?" and that using someone else's login is against our rules, whoever asks. I reported it to the office manager the same day, and I will speak to Payal tomorrow. — Nikhil, floor supervisor

qa.q: Whose login did Deepak use to enter the figures?
qa.a: Deepak used Payal's login to enter the client figures again.

qa.q: Why did Deepak say "Payal said it was fine" when Nikhil asked?
qa.a: Deepak was moving responsibility onto the senior analyst and felt anxious about a bad reference, which is why he complied without asking.

qa.q: What turning point in Nikhil's private talk could help Deepak next time?
qa.a: Nikhil told Deepak it is fine to ask "is this okay?" and that the rule applies whoever asks, which gives Deepak words to use and takes away the fear of asking.

qa.q: How might Payal see the situation?
qa.a: Payal may have been under deadline pressure and thought of the shortcut as small, without noticing how a new intern would feel unable to say no.

grounding: A new intern does what a senior instructs to gain favour or avoid trouble, feeling that responsibility has moved to the person giving the order.

subtype: Following a boss into a grey area [Actor]
passage: I am Sabina, and this is about the form I backdated. Wasim, my manager, came to my desk on a Friday. "Just put last Monday's date on the safety checklist. The inspection is Tuesday, and it was done anyway, more or less." Two colleagues were within earshot, and one looked up and then down at a screen. I said "Okay" before my brain caught up. I told myself it was his call and he was the one signing. I typed the old date, and my hands felt oddly cold. That night I realised nobody had forced me. I had simply been handed a way not to decide.

qa.q: Which date did Sabina type on the safety checklist?
qa.a: Sabina typed last Monday's date on the safety checklist.

qa.q: Why did Sabina say "Okay" before thinking it through?
qa.a: Sabina felt the decision belonged to Wasim, which brought a brief relief; the cold hands suggest an uneasy sense that this was not really acceptable.

qa.q: What could Sabina have done at the desk instead of saying "Okay"?
qa.a: Sabina could have asked "is this okay?", asked for the request in writing, or taken the question to the proper channel, since following a request does not remove personal responsibility.

qa.q: How might the colleague who looked up and then down have been feeling?
qa.a: That colleague may have felt uncomfortable but unwilling to step in, assuming, like Sabina, that it was not their decision to make.

grounding: An employee complies with a manager's request to backdate a form, telling themselves it is not their decision, with responsibility diffused.

subtype: Following a boss into a grey area [Actor]
passage: Compliance note, Thursday. Samir, a junior engineer, changed two readings in the site report after his manager Vidya said, "Smooth it, the client is nervous." In the corridor Samir told me, "It was not my decision," and looked relieved and sick at the same time. The two others on the team said they knew but had not thought it was theirs to raise. I told Samir that a request from a manager does not remove personal responsibility and that he can ask for it in writing. The same day I raised the report with the head of quality, who has asked for the original readings to be restored. — Naveen, compliance officer

qa.q: How many readings did Samir change in the site report?
qa.a: Samir changed two readings in the site report.

qa.q: What does Samir's look of being relieved and sick at once suggest about how Samir feels?
qa.a: It suggests guilt mixed with relief: saying "It was not my decision" moves the weight elsewhere, yet Samir knows the change was wrong.

qa.q: What steps did Naveen take that put Samir on a safer footing?
qa.a: Naveen told Samir personal responsibility remains and to ask for such requests in writing, and raised the report with the head of quality the same day so the readings could be restored.

qa.q: Why might the two others on the team have stayed silent although they knew?
qa.a: They may have felt it was not theirs to raise, each assuming someone else or the manager would handle it; the responsibility was spread thin between them.

grounding: An employee smooths a report at a manager's request, telling themselves it is not their decision, as diffused responsibility does.

passage: In the district cooperative office, Nandini was collecting tea cups when she saw Samir stamping loan forms that had no signature on the last page. "Sir said to push them through today," Samir muttered without looking up. The clerk at the next desk, Ravi, kept typing, and the peon shuffled out. Nandini put the cups down. She did not say "you are wrong". She said, "Samir, is this okay?" The stamp stopped in the air. "I thought..." Samir began, and then, "I will check with Sir." Samir set the pile aside and, for the first time that afternoon, looked at her.

qa.q: What was missing from the loan forms Samir was stamping?
qa.a: The loan forms had no signature on the last page.

qa.q: What might Samir be feeling when the stamp stops in the air after Nandini's question?
qa.a: Samir may feel caught off guard and a little uneasy, but also relieved to be given room to pause; there is no sign of being accused.

qa.q: Why did Nandini's way of asking work, and what else could she add?
qa.a: A plain question left Samir room to think instead of defend, and Nandini could also offer to go with Samir to check with the manager.

qa.q: Why might Ravi have kept typing while Samir stamped?
qa.a: Ravi may have noticed but not felt it was the place, or assumed someone else would say something; staying busy is an easy way to avoid the question.

grounding: A person sees a peer quietly doing something dubious on instruction and asks a plain question, giving space to pause without accusation.

passage: At a Rotterdam warehouse loading bay, Kofi noticed Gabriel peeling expiry labels off pallets of yoghurt and sticking on new ones. Anke, the supervisor, had just walked past saying, "Make it ready for the morning trucks." Two forklift drivers pretended not to see. Kofi walked over with two coffees and said, "Hey, is this okay?" Gabriel froze, holding a label. "Anke said..." "I know. I just wondered." After a moment Gabriel put the label down. "Maybe I should ask her properly." Kofi handed over a coffee and said he would come along.

qa.q: What was Gabriel doing to the pallets of yoghurt?
qa.a: Gabriel was peeling expiry labels off the pallets and sticking on new ones.

qa.q: What might Gabriel be feeling when freezing with a label in hand?
qa.a: Gabriel may feel startled and worried, caught between following Anke's words and a doubt that the job is right.

qa.q: What did Kofi do that gave Gabriel space to stop?
qa.a: Kofi brought coffee, asked a plain "is this okay?" without accusing, and offered to go along, so Gabriel could pause without being blamed.

qa.q: Why might the two forklift drivers have pretended not to see?
qa.a: They may have felt it was not their job or feared trouble with Anke, so ignoring it was the easier way to avoid deciding.

grounding: A person sees a peer doing something dubious on instruction, and a plain question lets the person pause without being accused.

passage: My name is Anand. Last spring my manager Pooja asked me to change the supplier's invoice date so the payment would look on time. She said it kindly, as if it were nothing. My face went warm. I said, "Can you send me that in an email, so I have it clear?" She laughed and told me not to be so formal. I said I would still prefer it in writing. She went quiet. Two teammates, Rohit and Zara, kept their eyes on their screens. That evening I emailed the finance controller a plain question about the correct procedure. No drama. Pooja did not speak to me for two days, and then she nodded at me in the lift.

qa.q: What did Pooja ask Anand to change?
qa.a: Pooja asked Anand to change the supplier's invoice date.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when asking for the request in writing?
qa.a: Anand felt nervous, with a warm face, but resolved; the calm repetition "in writing" shows Anand was determined not to be swept along.

qa.q: Which steps did Anand use to decline without a fight?
qa.a: Anand asked for the instruction in writing and then sent a plain question about the correct procedure to the finance controller, using the proper channel instead of arguing.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt when Anand asked for the request in writing?
qa.a: Pooja may have felt caught out or irritated; going quiet and not speaking for two days suggests discomfort before the nod in the lift.

grounding: An adult declines an improper instruction calmly, asks for it in writing and uses a proper channel, knowing orders do not remove responsibility.

passage: Note from the department head, Lalit. On Wednesday a director told Gargi, in front of the analysis team, to remove a warning line from the quarterly report. Gargi said calmly, "I can do that if you send the instruction in writing, and I would like the compliance team to see the report first." The room went silent. Two analysts looked at me. The director walked out. I stood by Gargi's request, and that afternoon I passed the matter to compliance myself and told the analysts this is how a query should be handled. Gargi did not raise her voice once.

qa.q: What did the director tell Gargi to remove from the report?
qa.a: The director told Gargi to remove a warning line from the quarterly report.

qa.q: What does Gargi's calm request for the instruction in writing suggest about how Gargi feels?
qa.a: It suggests Gargi feels steady and sure of the proper route, without needing to win or accuse anyone, since Gargi did not raise a voice once.

qa.q: What turning point in Lalit's response backed Gargi up?
qa.a: Lalit stood by the request and passed the matter to compliance that afternoon, which showed the analysts the proper channel in action.

qa.q: What might the two analysts who looked at Lalit have been feeling?
qa.a: They may have felt tense and unsure, checking whether the head would support Gargi or the director; they were waiting to see what was safe.

grounding: An adult refuses an improper instruction calmly, asks for it in writing and uses proper channels, a case of personal responsibility surviving orders.

passage: My name is Jomon, and I was in the treasure hunt team. Jeevan said, "We start at the big tree, follow me!" and everyone ran after him. Gauri whispered, "I think the clue means the water tap, not the tree." I heard her, but Jeevan was already far ahead and I did not want to stop the game or make him angry. So I ran to the tree too. We dug around the roots for a long time. The other team found the box at the tap. Gauri did not say "I told you." She just looked at her shoes, and I felt bad.

qa.q: Where did Gauri think the clue pointed?
qa.a: Gauri thought the clue meant the water tap, not the tree.

qa.q: Why did Jomon run to the tree after hearing Gauri?
qa.a: Jomon did not want to stop the game or make Jeevan angry, so keeping the fun and the friendship felt more important than checking; later Jomon felt bad.

qa.q: What could Jomon have done at the moment Gauri whispered?
qa.a: Jomon could have called out "Wait, Gauri has an idea" and asked the team to check both places before digging.

qa.q: How might Gauri feel after the other team found the box at the tap?
qa.a: Gauri may feel disappointed and unheard; looking at her shoes and not saying "I told you" suggests hurt but no wish to blame anyone.

grounding: Children follow the confident child's plan even when a quieter child has a better idea, since arguing seems to risk the fun and the friendship.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 5 relay practice. Uma, always sure of herself, announced the running order and the team fell in line. Tara, the quietest, said softly that Kabir should run last as he was faster at the finish. Nobody replied, and Uma had already moved on. The team came third. Afterwards nobody would say why. Next time I asked each child to name one idea before the order was decided, and told the group that a good plan can come from anyone. Tara nodded and looked surprised to be asked. — Jagdish Sir

qa.q: Who suggested that Kabir should run last?
qa.a: Tara suggested that Kabir should run last.

qa.q: Why did nobody reply when Tara spoke softly about the running order?
qa.a: The team was following Uma's confident lead and nobody wanted to interrupt the plan or risk the fun and the friendship, so Tara's idea slipped past unnoticed.

qa.q: What did Jagdish Sir change that gave a quiet child a chance?
qa.a: Jagdish Sir asked each child to name one idea before the order was decided and said a good plan can come from anyone.

qa.q: How might Tara have experienced being unheard, and then being asked?
qa.a: Tara probably felt overlooked the first time, and the surprised nod when asked suggests being invited to speak was new and welcome.

grounding: Children follow the confident child's plan even when a quieter child has a better idea, and nobody checks for fear of spoiling the game.

passage: "Open-air quiz on the terrace, four o'clock, in May," said Mehak. "Done?" "Done!" said Ritesh at once. "Sounds great," said Pia. "Fine with me," said Karan. Hansa, holding the pen, looked at the sun burning on the window. It will be very hot at four, she thought. "Hansa? Minutes?" "Yes. Open-air, four o'clock, May." She wrote it down. "Perfect," said Mehak. "Meeting over." Ritesh grabbed his bag. In the corridor Hansa whispered to Pia, "Do you think the terrace will be too hot?" "I was thinking the same," said Pia, "but nobody said."

qa.q: What time and month did Mehak propose for the quiz?
qa.a: Mehak proposed a quiz on the terrace at four o'clock in May.

qa.q: Why did Hansa write down the plan without mentioning the heat?
qa.a: Hansa did not want to spoil the mood or be the only doubter, so the worry stayed inside; the whisper in the corridor shows the doubt was real.

qa.q: What could the committee do differently at the moment Mehak says "Done?"
qa.a: Someone could ask "Does anyone see a problem?" or set a short pause, so doubts like the heat can be raised before the plan is fixed.

qa.q: What might it be like for Pia, who had the same doubt but said "Sounds great"?
qa.a: Pia probably feels a little regretful and relieved on finding Hansa thought the same; the quick agreement hid a doubt that two people held.

grounding: A group of teens planning an event rushes to agree with the loudest member, and doubts stay unspoken so a poor plan goes ahead.

passage: I am Pooja, and I was on the cultural committee in Class 11. Dilnaz loves big ideas, and at the meeting she said, "Let us do forty stalls and a stage show on the same day." Everyone clapped. I was thinking about volunteers, because we barely had twelve. But the room was happy, Dilnaz was glowing, and I did not want to be the one who said no. So I said, "Great idea." Three others told me later that they had been worried too. Five days before the fete we still had no volunteers, and half the stalls were empty tables. Dilnaz looked at me and asked, "Why did nobody say anything?" I had no answer.

qa.q: How many volunteers did the committee barely have?
qa.a: The committee barely had twelve volunteers.

qa.q: Why did Pooja say "Great idea" while thinking about volunteers?
qa.a: Pooja did not want to be the one who spoiled the happy mood, so a real worry stayed unspoken; the feeling was a wish to keep the peace.

qa.q: What might Pooja have done at the meeting to raise the concern without spoiling the mood?
qa.a: Pooja could have said "I love it, can we check how many volunteers we need?", turning the doubt into a practical question.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel when asking "Why did nobody say anything?"
qa.a: Dilnaz may feel surprised and a bit hurt, having believed everyone shared the excitement; the question suggests Dilnaz wants honest views next time.

grounding: A group of teens rushes to agree with the loudest member, doubts stay unspoken and a poor plan goes ahead.

passage: Faculty guide's note, third-year project review. The team led by Dhruv presented sensor readings that jumped erratically. Manjula said that the sensor might need recalibrating and the data should be rechecked. Dhruv smiled and said, "We have been over this, we are on track." The other three members nodded. Manjula stopped speaking and looked at her laptop. The team seemed very close and confident, which made the concern sound like disloyalty. I asked the team to re-run one test with Manjula's suggestion before the next meeting, and I asked Manjula privately to keep sharing what she notices. — Prof. Rao

qa.q: Who said the sensor might need recalibrating?
qa.a: Manjula said the sensor might need recalibrating and the data should be rechecked.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv smile and say "We are on track"?
qa.a: Dhruv felt confident and united with the team, and treated the concern as a threat to the group's togetherness instead of as useful information.

qa.q: What did the guide do that gave the concern a fair hearing?
qa.a: The guide asked the team to re-run one test with Manjula's suggestion and asked Manjula privately to keep sharing observations.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel after the team nodded along with Dhruv?
qa.a: Manjula may feel discouraged and isolated; stopping speaking and looking at the laptop suggests unsureness about whether the concern is welcome.

grounding: A college project team dismisses a member's concern because the group feels united and confident, treating contrary evidence as disloyalty.

passage: Thursday. Our team meeting went so well. We are a proper unit now, five of us finishing each other's sentences. Avni said the survey only covers our own hostel and might not show anything general. I said, "You always worry too much," and everyone laughed, even Avni after a moment, though it was not a real laugh. Tejas said, "So we are all agreed." We printed the report. I felt so proud of us. But tonight I cannot stop seeing Avni's face when she picked up her bag. Maybe I should ask her. But it would spoil the mood. — Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Avni say about the survey?
qa.a: Avni said the survey only covers our own hostel and might not show anything general.

qa.q: What is Dilnaz feeling by the end of the entry?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels pride mixed with unease; not being able to stop seeing Avni's face shows a doubt underneath the good feeling about the team.

qa.q: What choice could Dilnaz make about the survey and Avni's worry?
qa.a: Dilnaz could ask Avni what worries her about the sample and bring it back to the team before more copies are printed.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when everyone laughed at the worry?
qa.a: Avni may have felt dismissed and awkward; laughing after a moment in a way that was not real suggests hiding hurt to keep the peace.

grounding: A college project team dismisses a member's concern because the group feels united, and the mood is protected over the evidence.

passage: Dear Rukmini, I have to tell someone. In yesterday's seminar on the water project, everyone looked so certain. Even our professor said the budget looked fine. But I noticed that the maintenance cost was left out of the sheet. I kept my hand down. I thought: they are all clever, they must have counted it, and I would look silly. Afterwards, on the stairs, Meenal said, "Did nobody notice the maintenance line?" and Aakash said, "I did, but I thought I was missing something." Half of us had the same doubt and said nothing! I want to bring it up next week. Wish me courage. — Yamini

qa.q: What was left out of the budget sheet?
qa.a: The maintenance cost was left out of the sheet.

qa.q: Why did Yamini keep a hand down in the seminar?
qa.a: Everyone else looked certain, so Yamini assumed the others knew better and feared looking silly; the feeling was doubt turned into self-silencing.

qa.q: What turning point does Yamini choose after the stairs conversation?
qa.a: Yamini decides to bring the maintenance question up next week, having learned that others held the same doubt.

qa.q: What might Aakash have been thinking when saying "I thought I was missing something"?
qa.a: Aakash probably assumed the group must have a reason and that the doubt showed a gap in Aakash's own understanding, so silence seemed safer than asking.

grounding: A student keeps a reservation private because everyone looks certain, not realising several others are silent for the same reason.

passage: Deepak, it's me, Sunaina. Remember the pitch review last week? The whole room was nodding. The slide said two hundred sign-ups, and I had this tiny voice saying that number looks made up. But everyone looked so sure, even Vikram, who is the sharpest of us. So I decided I was the one who did not understand. I stayed silent and even nodded. After the meeting Rina said in the lift, "I thought the number looked odd too," and then Kunal said, "Me too!" I nearly laughed. Three of us had swallowed the same doubt for an hour. Deepak, I am going to say something at the next one, even if my voice shakes.

qa.q: How many sign-ups did the slide claim?
qa.a: The slide said two hundred sign-ups.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina decide to be silent and even nod in the meeting?
qa.a: Sunaina thought everyone else looked sure, so the doubt must be Sunaina's own misunderstanding; it was self-doubt more than agreement.

qa.q: What choice does Sunaina make at the end of the story?
qa.a: Sunaina decides to say something at the next review even if the voice shakes, having learned that others had the same doubt.

qa.q: What might Kunal have felt when saying "Me too!" in the lift?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt relief and surprise at finding out the doubt was shared, after an hour of holding it alone.

grounding: A student keeps a doubt to themselves because everyone else looks certain, not realising others are silent for the same reason.

passage: I was on the same project team and watched Vasudha do something clever. Before Monday's meeting she messaged us: "Please write down any worries and drop them in the shared sheet by tonight, no names needed." Arnab, who usually talks first and fastest, said it was a waste of time. But most of us did it. On Monday, when the sheet was projected, seven of the ten worries were about the same delivery date. Arnab read them, went quiet, then said, "Okay, that is a real problem." Jiya, a first-year intern who never speaks in meetings, whispered to me, "I wrote the third one." I could not tell whether Arnab was annoyed, but he changed the schedule.

qa.q: How many of the ten worries were about the same delivery date?
qa.a: Seven of the ten worries were about the same delivery date.

qa.q: What might Jiya be feeling when whispering "I wrote the third one"?
qa.a: Jiya probably feels proud and relieved that a worry got heard, since speaking aloud in meetings is hard and writing it down felt safe.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha's suggestion help quieter people, and what might strengthen it further?
qa.a: Collecting worries privately before the group mood formed let quiet voices be heard; the team could also start meetings by reading the sheet out before anyone comments.

qa.q: What might the meeting have been like for Arnab, who usually talks first?
qa.a: Arnab may have felt surprised or uncomfortable at first, but reading the sheet and changing the schedule suggests he accepted the evidence.

grounding: A team member suggests everyone note their concerns privately before the meeting, so quiet voices are not drowned out.

passage: Tuesday. The final-year project group was about to vote on the demo plan. Nitin, the team lead, said it would be a shame to argue, so nobody argued. Sonali had a doubt about the battery but did not say it. Friday. The doubt still nagged, so Sonali asked everyone to write concerns on paper before Monday's talk. Nitin sighed but agreed. Monday. Six slips lay on the table. Four mentioned the battery. Nitin read them aloud and said, "I would not have heard this if we had just discussed." The group tested the battery that week. Sonali quietly kept the slips in a folder.

qa.q: How many of the six slips mentioned the battery?
qa.a: Four of the six slips mentioned the battery.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling on Tuesday and again on Friday?
qa.a: Sonali felt uneasy, with a doubt that was held back on Tuesday and that kept nagging by Friday, until the worry was strong enough to act on.

qa.q: What did Sonali change between Tuesday and Monday that made a difference?
qa.a: Sonali asked everyone to write concerns on paper before the talk, so views were collected before the group's mood formed.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt while reading the slips aloud?
qa.a: Nitin may have felt surprised and a little humbled; saying "I would not have heard this" in a plain discussion shows the written slips proved their worth.

grounding: A team member suggests everyone note their concerns privately before the meeting, which keeps quiet voices from being drowned out.

passage: Thursday. The whole team nodded through the new launch plan today. Tejas presented it with such confidence that saying anything felt rude. I had three worries: the timing, the budget and the vendor. I said nothing. Neither did anyone else, and Meera even said, "Love it." Afterwards at the water cooler Meera whispered, "Did anyone actually think this would work?" Then Sameer joined and said, "I was up all night worrying about the vendor." Almost everyone had doubts. Ten heads nodded and hardly one meant it. I felt oddly relieved and embarrassed at the same time. Tomorrow I will write my three worries down and send them to Tejas. — Divyansh

qa.q: What did Sameer say kept the night awake?
qa.a: Sameer said "I was up all night worrying about the vendor."

qa.q: What is Divyansh feeling after the water-cooler talk?
qa.a: Divyansh feels relieved that the doubts were shared and embarrassed that nobody said so in the meeting, a mixed state.

qa.q: What choice does Divyansh make for the next day?
qa.a: Divyansh decides to write the three worries down and send them to Tejas, which turns a private doubt into something that can be discussed.

qa.q: What might Meera be feeling, having said "Love it" and then whispering "Did anyone actually think this would work?"
qa.a: Meera probably feels uneasy and a little guilty, having agreed aloud while doubting, and relieved to find the others were unsure too.

grounding: A team nods through a plan while each person privately has worries, and hallway chats reveal that the unity was an illusion.
